easy.heading: Warming Up with Some Quick Sums
easy.body:
Starting today's easy grid was all about finding those small target numbers first. I looked straight at that sum region for 5 in the middle and the sum of 9 on the left. The trick was realizing that the dominoes like [2,5] and [3,5] were our heavy hitters. I placed the [3,5] domino at [2,2] and [2,3] because it fit the sum of 5 perfectly at the bottom while giving me a starting point for the bigger sum of 7 nearby.

Once that was in place, the rest fell like, well, dominoes! I used the [4,4] domino for the sum of 9, combining it with a 1 from the [0,1] domino. It felt really satisfying to see the grid fill up so quickly. If you got stuck, the empty spots at [1,1] and [2,1] were actually your best friends because they didn't force any math on you, giving you more wiggle room to place the [2,5] and [0,1] pairs.

medium.heading: The Double Ten Double Cross
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today was a bit of a brain teaser because of those two separate regions that both needed to sum up to 10. I spent a good few minutes staring at [1,3], [1,4] and [3,3], [3,4]. Since we only had one [5,5] domino, I knew it had to go in one of those spots, but which one? I eventually realized that the equals constraint at [2,0], [2,1], and [2,2] was the real key. It forced a pattern that only worked if I put the [5,5] domino in the top sum region.

Working through the middle was the hardest part. That equals sign means all three cells must have the same number of pips. I tried using 6s at first, but it made the sum of 6 at [0,2] and [1,2] impossible to finish. Once I switched tactics and used the [6,6] domino for the equals region and balanced it with the [3,6] and [3,1] dominoes, everything clicked. It just goes to show that sometimes you have to work from the middle of the board outward.

hard.heading: Cracking the Tiny Total Code
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today really lived up to its name! The absolute biggest challenge was that huge region at the bottom involving [5,4], [6,2], [6,3], and [6,4]. Having four cells that must sum to less than 5 is incredibly restrictive. It basically means you have to use almost all 1s and 0s. I had to restart twice because I kept accidentally using up my low-value dominoes like [1,1] too early in the top half of the board.

The breakthrough came when I looked at the sum of 10 near the top right. Since [0,3] and [0,4] had to hit 10, and one of them was part of a sum of 1 for [0,1] and [0,2], I knew I was looking for a very specific pairing. By placing the [1,6] and [0,4] dominoes carefully at the top, it freed up the [1,1] and [2,1] pairs for that tricky bottom section. It was a real exercise in patience, but man, it felt good to finally see that solved message pop up!

explanation.tips: Always start by looking for the most restrictive regions, like very small sums or long equals chains. If you see a sum of 10 or 11, you know you need your biggest dominoes there immediately. Also, don't forget that empty cells are just there to hold a domino side without any extra rules, so use them to park your awkward numbers.
explanation.learned: Today taught me how much one small region can affect the entire board, especially those less than constraints. In the hard puzzle, that sum of less than 5 at the bottom dictated almost every move I made in the top half because I had to save my small numbers. I also realized that equals regions are great for narrowing down which double dominoes like [4,4] or [6,6] go where.

faqs.question: What does a sum target mean in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: A sum target is a specific number located in a bolded region. All the pips in the cells within that region must add up exactly to that target number.

faqs.question: How do equals regions work in the Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: When you see an equals sign in a region, it means every single cell inside that bolded area must contain the exact same number of pips.

faqs.question: What are the rules for greater than and less than signs?
faqs.answer: A greater than sign means the pips in that specific cell must be more than the target number shown. A less than sign means the pips must be fewer than the target number.

faqs.question: Can I use the same domino twice in one puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, each puzzle gives you a specific set of unique dominoes. Once you use a domino like [2,5], you cannot use another [2,5] in that same grid.

faqs.question: What is an empty region in Pips?
faqs.answer: An empty region is an area with a bold border but no number or symbol inside. This means the cells don't have a specific math rule, but they still must be filled by dominoes following the standard layout rules.
